title: Google's Gemma 4 answers from a TPU in orbit
dek: Google says its Project Suncatcher satellite generated a Gemma 4 response in orbit, an early milestone in testing whether data-center AI hardware can operate in space.
whatHappened: On October 30, 2026, Google reported that its Project Suncatcher prototype had generated a Gemma 4 response in orbit earlier that week.
A ground station sent a prompt requesting a space-themed haiku; the satellite returned the result while passing Svalbard, Norway.
Google calls it the first AI response from a data-center-class TPU in orbit; the prototype satellite launched on October 1.
Thermal-stress and radiation tests are next, ahead of a planned twin-satellite milestone in 2027.
whyItMatters: The energy attraction predates this test: in its September 24 explanation, Google says low-Earth-orbit satellites can receive near-continuous sunlight. That motivates solar-powered AI infrastructure, but this response does not measure its delivered computing cost.

Cooling remains a constraint, not a free benefit of space. Google describes using heat pipes and radiators because the vacuum provides no airflow to carry heat away; sustained AI workloads must keep rejecting that heat.

The response tests an onboard model and the ground-to-satellite communication path. Scaling beyond one satellite also requires high-bandwidth links between moving spacecraft, which Google's September explanation identifies as a separate engineering challenge.
take: The meaningful step is that a data-center-class chip executed an AI workload after launch; the haiku's content tells us little about whether a fleet would be useful.

For infrastructure buyers, the next persuasive evidence would be sustained throughput per unit of power, reliable heat rejection and end-to-end costs including launch and replacement, rather than another short generated answer.
Until those numbers and inter-satellite links are demonstrated, orbital compute belongs in an engineering research budget rather than a production capacity plan.
openQuestions: Google has not established sustained throughput, service uptime, radiation-related failure rates or the cost of useful compute delivered to customers.
The October update does not report a working interconnected constellation or commercial availability; thermal, radiation and multi-satellite validation remain ahead.
